newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire battle front edges west, refugees flee.
newsitem.headline: Zaire battle front edges west, refugees flee.

text.p: Zaire's civil war battle front is edging further west with Tutsi-led rebels capturing the airstrip and refugee camp at Amisi, senior Zairean civil and military officials in the region say.
Witnesses say Rwandan Hutu refugees, Zairean civilians and demoralised soldiers have been fleeing ahead of the rebel advance compounding the problems of relief workers on the edge of the war zone.

But leaders of Hutus clustered round the village of Tingi Tingi show little apparent haste to return home to Rwanda, which accuses them of involvement in the 1994 genocide which killed an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

"The wind of panic is there. The war is getting nearer. Amisi is completely empty now," Innocent Seruntanga, a refugee coordinator in the make-shift Tingi Tingi camp about 75 km (45 miles) north west of Amisi, told Reuters.
Tingi Tingi, about 200 km (125 miles) south of the Kisangani headquarters of the counter-offensive Zaire launched on January 20, is temporary home to at least 127,000 Hutu refugees.
It has the largest single grouping of refugees in eastern Zaire. Kisangani is Zaire's third largest city.
All sides report fighting in the mining town of Punia, deep in the forest, on another route south of Tingi Tingi.

Witnesses said residents of nearby Lubutu and surrounding villages had started fleeing. One aid worker said the estimated 40,000 refugees from Amisi had halted about five km (three miles) south east of Tingi Tingi.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus.
They fled west in December following attacks on their camps. Hundreds of thousands of fellow Hutus opted to return home in December, trekking en masse in the opposite direction.
U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata, visiting Tingi Tingi on Saturday, told reporters accompanying her that the only solution for the refugees was to return home.

Ogata said she and the Zairean government had reached agreement on the principle of repatriating the remaining 300,000 or so Hutus. "The refugees have to move out. They have to go back home but it is not clear how, when and on what conditions."
But leaders of the Tingi Tingi refugees showed more interest in improving their conditions in Zaire than returning home.
Seruntanga said hunger may force some Hutus to return but he added: "Only a tiny minority may be willing to return home."
Ogata said the fast-moving front line posed a major threat to the refugees with the rebels taking Amisi.
"I am appealing to those who have information about the frontline. I would like to...know what the impending danger is. It's a huge concentration of people," Ogata said.
But rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday he would halt the advance on Tingi Tingi and target Kisangani instead.
Kabila reports successes in the north east and mineral-rich southern Shaba province. Zairean defence officials dispute some claims, concede others and claim successes of their own.

Relief agencies pulled international staff out of Tingi Tingi and Lubutu on Friday after soldiers demanding pay for pre-revolt work in refugee camps in the east shot dead an officer who intervened to stop them taking aid workers hostage.
"They went on a looting spree but that was quickly put down by well-disciplined soldiers," one aid official said. Foreign aid workers returned on Saturday. Ogata later left for Kenya.
